note.explanation: A stopwatch measures how long an event lasts. A mechanical stopwatch in this section has a least count of one tenth of a second. A digital stopwatch can measure one hundredth of a second.
note.checkAnswer: One tenth of a second (0.1 s).
note.simple: Use a stopwatch to measure how long something takes. Its least count tells you the smallest time interval it can measure.
note.checkQuestion: What is the least count of the mechanical stopwatch described in this section?
note.title: Measuring time with a stopwatch
steps: Press the knob to start the stopwatch.
Press the same knob to stop it when the event ends.
Read the time shown by the needles.
Press the knob again to return the needles to zero.
note.answer: A mechanical stopwatch measures an event's duration, and its least count is one tenth of a second.

options: 1 s
mcqs.stem: What is the least count of the mechanical stopwatch described in this section?
rationales: This is correct: each small division represents one tenth of a second.
This is incorrect: one second is larger than the smallest division described.
This is incorrect: one hundredth of a second is the capability stated for digital watches, not this mechanical stopwatch.
This is incorrect: ten seconds is not the value of one small division.

options: 30 big divisions, each divided into 10 small divisions
10 big divisions, each divided into 30 small divisions
30 small divisions, each divided into 10 big divisions
100 big divisions, each divided into 30 small divisions
mcqs.stem: How is the dial of the mechanical stopwatch usually divided?
rationales: This is correct: the section describes 30 big divisions, each further divided into 10 small divisions.
This is incorrect: it reverses the numbers of big and small divisions.
This is incorrect: it reverses which divisions are big and small.
This is incorrect: these are not the divisions described for the dial.

options: It measures the duration of an event.
It measures the mass of an object.
It measures the length of an object.
It measures the temperature of a substance.
mcqs.stem: What is a stopwatch used to measure?
rationales: This is correct: a stopwatch measures how long an event lasts.
This is incorrect: a stopwatch does not measure mass.
This is incorrect: a stopwatch does not measure length.
This is incorrect: a stopwatch does not measure temperature.

options: One hundredth of a second
One tenth of a second
One second
One minute
mcqs.stem: What part of a second can the electronic or digital watches mentioned in the section measure?
rationales: This is correct: the section says they can measure one hundredth part of a second.
This is incorrect: one tenth of a second is the mechanical stopwatch's least count.
This is incorrect: one second is not the smallest interval stated for the digital watches.
This is incorrect: one minute is much longer than the interval stated.

options: The knob is pressed to start and pressed again to stop it.
The knob is pressed once to start and the needles stop by themselves.
The knob is turned continuously to keep the stopwatch running.
The stopwatch is shaken to start and stop it.
mcqs.stem: How is the mechanical stopwatch started and stopped, according to the section?
rationales: This is correct: pressing the knob starts the watch, and pressing it again stops it.
This is incorrect: the section says the same knob is pushed to stop it.
This is incorrect: the section does not describe turning the knob continuously.
This is incorrect: shaking the stopwatch is not the stated method.

options: A sandclock
A metre rule
A measuring cylinder
A micrometer screw gauge
mcqs.stem: Which instrument in the section uses sand flowing from one chamber into another to indicate time?
rationales: This is correct: the sandclock uses sand flowing down from its upper chamber.
This is incorrect: a metre rule measures length, not time using flowing sand.
This is incorrect: a measuring cylinder measures volume, not time using flowing sand.
This is incorrect: a micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths, not time using flowing sand.

written.text: Suggest some natural phenomena that could serve as a reasonably accurate time standard.
written.finalAnswer: The rotation of the Earth and the revolution of the Earth around the Sun are natural periodic phenomena that could serve as time standards.

rubric.why: A natural repeating event is a possible basis for measuring time.
rubric.description: Names the Earth's rotation as a periodic phenomenon.
rubric.how: State that the Earth's rotation can be used as a time standard.

rubric.why: A second suitable periodic natural event completes the response.
rubric.description: Gives another suitable natural periodic phenomenon.
rubric.how: Name the Earth's revolution around the Sun, or another valid natural periodic phenomenon.

modelAnswer: The rotation of the Earth is a natural periodic phenomenon that could serve as a time standard.
The revolution of the Earth around the Sun is another natural periodic phenomenon that could serve as a time standard.

steps.why: The stopwatch must be started when the event begins.
steps.text: Press the knob on the top of the stopwatch to start it.

steps.why: Stopping the watch at the end of the event gives its duration.
steps.text: Push the same knob again to stop it.

steps.why: The needle positions show the measured time.
Returning the needles to zero prepares the stopwatch for the next measurement.
steps.text: Press the same knob again to bring the needles back to zero.

example.question: How is a mechanical stopwatch used to measure the duration of an event?
example.answer: Press the knob to start the stopwatch, press it again to stop it, note the reading, and press it again to return the needles to zero.

explain.title: What a stopwatch measures
explain.body: The duration of time of an event is measured by a stopwatch as shown in Fig. 1.10.

explain.title: The mechanical stopwatch's least count
explain.body: Each small division represents one tenth (1/10) of a second. Thus, one tenth of a second is the least count of this stopwatch.

explain.title: Digital watches
explain.body: Now-a-days, electronic/digital watches (Fig. 1.11) are also available which can measure one hundredth part of a second.

explain.title: A sandclock activity
explain.body: Using two glass funnels, adhesive tape, two lids, and dry sand, observe how much time it takes for the sand to flow down once completely. Make a paper scale from this and paste on the glass funnels along straight side.

mistakes: Do not confuse the mechanical stopwatch's least count of 0.1 s with the digital watch's ability to measure 0.01 s.
Do not forget to multiply by 60 for minutes and by 60 again for hours when converting time to seconds.
For the exercise's month calculation, do not use a different number of days; the printed answer uses 30 days.
When writing scientific notation, keep the number before the power of ten at least 1 and less than 10.
